video.title: Fix Your Forehand Over-Rotation | 3 Counter-Rotational Balance Techniques

classification.reason: The coach explains the mechanics of counter-rotational braking on the forehand to fix over-rotation and demonstrates three specific technical variations.

problem.title_as_question: How can you fix forehand over-rotation using counter-rotational balance techniques?
problem.definition: Players spin continuously through the ball instead of using counter-rotational braking to stop hip rotation, resulting in lower power, reduced accuracy, and loss of balance.
prerequisites: loading into the hip or legs

symptoms.description: Hitting the ball slower and with less accuracy due to lack of rotational control.
The body spins out past the shot instead of staying on a linear path through contact.
The front foot and heel lift off the ground prematurely during contact instead of resisting rotation.
Shanking the forehand wide or having the chest flare open through contact.

causes.statement: Hip rotation is treated as a continuous twisting movement all the way through contact rather than a transient start-and-stop motion.
The hitting leg fails to kick back behind the body during forward weight transfer on attacking shots to break the hip rotation.
The free non-hitting leg is not utilized to kick up or across to counterbalance and brake the initial rotational force.
The player fails to exert static downward force into the ground through the front foot to brace and resist outward rotation through contact.

angles.summary: Forehand hip rotation must be transient: the counter-rotational break halts the hips to create a whip effect that snaps the torso through the hitting zone.
Roger Federer hits identical inside-out forehands by seamlessly alternating between a right-leg kick back and a left-leg kick up.
MLB pitchers like Jacob deGrom firmly block and rotate their front knee back in at release to convert rotational energy into linear momentum, analogous to contact in tennis.
The coach demonstrates missing wide when the front foot prematurely unweights and twists, contrasted with holding the foot planted to stabilize the shot.
Players often assume jumping off the front foot occurs during contact, whereas pros remain planted through contact and only hop on the follow-through.

solutions.summary: Practice early swing driving and braking motions with a medicine ball to leverage heavy kinesthetic feedback until the movements become habitual.
solutions.external_goal: Feel the added resistance of the medicine ball to coordinate the lower body breaking action.

solutions.summary: Check that the front foot remains planted and actively pressing back against the ground through contact, delaying any hop until the follow-through.
solutions.external_goal: Keep the front foot and heel attached to the ground through the hitting zone.
